sections.title: The Prohibition of Idolatry for Bnei Noaḥ
sections.html:
Idolatry is forbidden to all human beings, for there is no transgression that diverts a person's mind from truth to falsehood and from good to evil more than idolatry. It is therefore agreed that it is the first mitzva, which Adam, the first man, was already commanded.

The law for a ben Noaḥ (a descendant of Noah, i.e. a non-Jew) is like the law for a Jew: one who worships idols is liable to death. However, as we have learned (above 3:2), the main intent of this is to express the severity of the sin under the laws of Heaven, but in practice the attitude toward people who committed this sin is complex. For just as there are mitzvot whose punishment is death, such as idolatry, so there are many mitzvot that earn a person life, and the overall reckoning for each person is made in the Heavenly Court. And just as God desires the good of all His creatures, so it is fitting for the righteous to do good to idol worshippers as well and to draw them closer to faith in God. This is how Avraham Avinu acted: he related to everyone with love and sought out guests to bring them into his home, honour them with food and drink and draw them closer to faith, even though in his days everyone worshipped idols. He acted this way even toward lowly idol worshippers who worshipped the dust of their feet (Rashi, Bereishit 18:4). This is also evident from the fact that he pleaded in defence of the people of Sodom, who, in addition to all their grave sins, certainly also worshipped idols.1

In the definition of worship, too, the law for Bnei Noaḥ is like the law for Jews: the grave prohibition whose punishment is death is to declare acceptance of the idol as a god, or to worship it in the manner of worship particular to it, or in one of the four important services that were performed in the Temple, which are: 1) bowing down; 2) slaughtering a sacrifice; 3) burning a sacrifice on the altar; 4) pouring a libation of wine, or sprinkling blood and the like, in honour of the idol.

As for Jews, so for a ben Noaḥ it is forbidden to express honour or affection for an idol even when this is done not in the manner of worship customary for that idol, such as hugging the statue, kissing it or sweeping before it. But one is not liable to death for this. Likewise, it is forbidden for a ben Noaḥ to make a statue, but one who makes it is not liable to death (Sanhedrin 56b and Meiri there; Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 9:2; above 3:3).2

sections.title: Between Israel and the Nations in Faith and Kiddush Hashem
sections.html:
Although all human beings are commanded to believe in God and not to worship idols, the mitzva of faith obligates Israel more than the other nations. For Israel were chosen by God to reveal His light and blessing in the world, and for this purpose He made a covenant with them at Mount Sinai and gave them the Torah, and warned them about faith in His unity in a special way. Thus it is stated (Devarim 6:4-5): "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might." "With all your soul – even if He takes your soul" (Mishna Berakhot 9:5; above 4:1).

Therefore the people of Israel are commanded regarding kiddush Hashem (sanctification of God's Name): if a Jew is coerced to worship idols, he is obligated to be killed rather than worship them, whereas a ben Noaḥ is not obligated to give up his life for this, and he is permitted to worship rather than be killed. As it is stated (Vayikra 22:31): "You shall not profane My holy Name, and I shall be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel." The Sages said: "Israel are commanded regarding kiddush Hashem, and the non-Jews are not commanded regarding kiddush Hashem" (Yerushalmi, Sanhedrin 3:5). Therefore, if a Jew is coerced to bow down to a statue, even in private, he must be killed rather than transgress. Not only that, but even if he is coerced to give honour to an idol in a manner that is not its main worship, such as hugging or kissing it, he must be killed rather than transgress (above 4:4). But if a ben Noaḥ is coerced, even in public, to bow down to a statue and worship it, he need not give up his life, for as long as he continues to believe in God in his heart, he may outwardly worship the idol and not be killed (Rambam, Hilkhot Melakhim 10:2; Tosafot and Ran).

We also learn this from the blessing of Elisha the prophet to Na'aman, the general of the army of Aram. Na'aman suffered from tzara'at, and after he immersed seven times in the Jordan as Elisha the prophet instructed, he recognised "that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel" (II Melakhim 5:15), and he took upon himself to serve God and to refrain from idolatry. However, he went on to say to Elisha apologetically that when he went with his king to the idol worship in the house of Rimon, he would be forced to bow down with him to the statue. Elisha blessed him, "Go in peace," implying that he bore no prohibition, since he was doing so under duress. As it is stated (ibid. 5:17-19): "And Na'aman said… for your servant will no longer offer burnt offering or sacrifice to other gods, but only to the Lord. In this matter may the Lord pardon your servant: when my master (my king) comes into the house of Rimon (idolatry) to bow down there, and he leans on my hand, and I bow down in the house of Rimon – when I bow down in the house of Rimon, may the Lord [please] pardon your servant in this matter. And he said to him: Go in peace."3

sections.title: The Difference in the Temple
sections.html:
From a Jewish apostate, that is, a Jew who worships idols, a sacrifice is not accepted, but from a ben Noaḥ, even if he worships idols, a sacrifice is accepted. As it is stated (Vayikra 1:2): "When a man of you brings an offering," and the Sages expounded (Ḥullin 5a): "'Of you' – but not all of you, to exclude the apostate. 'Of you' – among you I made a distinction, but not among the nations," meaning that from members of the nations a sacrifice is accepted even when they worship idols. It is also stated (ibid. 17:8): "Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who offers a burnt offering," and the Sages expounded (Ḥullin 13b): "'Any man' (ish ish) – to include idolaters, who vow vows and freewill offerings like Israel." (The sacrifices accepted from non-Jews are burnt offerings; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aseh Ha-korbanot 3:2-4.)

Similarly, we learn that when King Shlomo finished building the Temple, he prayed to God to rest His Presence upon the Temple, and asked that when Israel come to pray in the Temple, God answer their prayer according to what they deserve by their deeds and the purity of their hearts. As it is stated (I Melakhim 8:38-39): "Whatever prayer, whatever supplication there may be from any man of all Your people Israel… then hear in heaven, Your dwelling place, and forgive and act, and give to each man according to all his ways, whose heart You know." But when a non-Jew comes to pray before God, Shlomo asked that God always hear his prayer, so that he would be strengthened in his faith. As it is stated (ibid. 8:41-43): "Also the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel, and comes from a distant land for Your Name's sake… and comes and prays toward this house – hear in heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all that the foreigner calls to You for, so that all the peoples of the earth may know Your Name, to fear You as do Your people Israel, and to know that Your Name is called upon this house that I have built." The commentators explained that Shlomo asked that God answer the prayer of non-Jews even though their hearts are not whole in their faith, and even if they were idol worshippers, in order to draw them closer (Rashi, Radak, Abarbanel, Alshikh, Malbim).

sections.title: The Mitzva to Eradicate Idolatry and the Prohibition of Benefit
sections.html:
The people of Israel are commanded to eradicate idolatry from the Land of Israel, and every individual Jew, whether in the Land or abroad, is likewise commanded to eradicate idolatry that has come into his possession (above 3:9-10). However, Bnei Noaḥ have no obligation to eradicate idolatry from their land, nor is an individual obligated to eradicate idolatry that has come into his possession.

A Jew is forbidden to derive benefit from an idol, from its service vessels or from the offerings brought to it; he is even forbidden to sell it and benefit from the proceeds. Rather, he is commanded to destroy it from the world (below 10:1-2). Bnei Noaḥ, however, not only have no mitzva to destroy an idol, but are even permitted to benefit from the proceeds of an idol and of everything associated with it. Thus it was instructed regarding one who was about to convert, that so as not to lose the value of his statues, he should sell them and receive the money for them while he is still a non-Jew, and afterwards convert (Avoda Zara 64a).4

sections.title: Prohibitions Specific to Israel
sections.html:
As we learned (3:5), the Torah warned Israel that one must not entice his fellow to worship idols. It was stringent in his punishment: even if in practice he did not succeed in persuading his fellow to worship idols, he is liable to death. It further warned not to pity him or have mercy on him, both in bringing him to court and in the court proceedings. However, a ben Noaḥ who enticed someone to worship idols, although he thereby transgressed a grave prohibition, is not liable to death, since the law of the mesit (enticer) does not apply to Bnei Noaḥ.5

As a safeguard to the prohibition of idolatry, the Torah commanded Israel not to make images of a human being, the sun, the moon, the stars and the ministering angels. This Torah prohibition applies even when there is no concern that they will want to worship them (below 15:1-7). Bnei Noaḥ, however, are not forbidden to make them; only when there is a concern that they will stumble into worshipping them is it forbidden for them to make them.

Likewise, in order to distance Israel from any trace of idolatry, the Torah forbade Israel to erect a pillar (matzeva) for the service of God, because idol worshippers were accustomed to do so. It also forbade planting a tree near the Temple, or bowing down outside the Temple on a figured stone (even maskit), because that is what idol worshippers did (below 15:11-13). For Bnei Noaḥ, however, there is no prohibition in this; only things that are liable to lead them to actually worship idols are forbidden.6

Israel were warned not to mention the name of an idol or to cause others to mention it, as it is stated (Shemot 23:13): "And you shall not mention the name of other gods; it shall not be heard on your mouth" (below 14:1), whereas for Bnei Noaḥ there is no prohibition in this (Ramban; SMA, ḤM 176:92).7

sections.title: The Lenient Attitude toward the Kutim
sections.html:
After the king of Assyria exiled Israel from Shomron and brought the Kutim (Samaritans) in their place, lions would kill the Kutim. "And they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying: The nations that you exiled and settled in the cities of Shomron do not know the law of the God of the land, and He has sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them, because they do not know the law of the God of the land. And the king of Assyria commanded, saying: Bring there one of the priests whom you exiled from there, and let them go and dwell there, and let him teach them the law of the God of the land. So one of the priests whom they had exiled from Shomron came and dwelt in Beit El, and he taught them how they should fear the Lord" (II Melakhim 17:26-28). "So these nations feared the Lord, and they also served their graven images, both their children and their children's children" (ibid. 17:41). And even though they associated the service of God with idolatry, the lions no longer killed them.

We learned two principles. The first: God is more exacting regarding idolatry in the Land of Israel than outside the Land, and therefore those Kutim who continued their practices in the Land were punished by the lions. The second: God is less exacting with Bnei Noaḥ than with Israel, and therefore as long as they combine faith in God with their idolatry, they are not punished.

Ramban explained that since God's providence over the nations is exercised indirectly, through angels and ministers appointed over them, He is not exacting with them when they err and worship those [powers] in their own lands. But in the Land of Israel, which is watched over by God, the exactingness toward them increases. Even so, they were not required to serve God alone as Israel are; rather, as long as they also feared God, even though they also worshipped idols, they were no longer punished (Vayikra 18:25; Derasha for Rosh Ha-shana; Recanati there; Responsa of Rashba Ha-ḥadashot 368; Rabbeinu Baḥya, Devarim 31:16; Alshikh, II Melakhim 17).

Radak expanded on this and explained (II Melakhim 17:28) that the priest who taught the Kutim did not try to prevent them from idolatry, because he knew they were incapable of it; rather, he taught them that the Lord is the God of gods, and thereby they were saved. Malbim added (there 28-41) that since Bnei Noaḥ did not stand in the covenant with God, they were not forbidden shituf, and therefore as long as they combine faith in God with their idolatry, their turning to God is desirable and they bear no sin.8

sections.title: Idolatry in Shituf for Israel
sections.html:
Idolatry in shituf (association) means that a person believes that the Lord is the God of gods, the source of the powers and the One capable of influencing them, and therefore he prays to Him. Yet at the same time he believes that God created various powers that govern the world, such as the forces of nature, and that they have an independent ability to influence what happens in the world, to do good or to do harm. And since they do good to those who revere them and harm those who do not worship them, he bows down to their statues and performs rites before them. In this way he associates with the service of God and faith in Him also faith in idols and their worship.

As we learned (above 3:4), for Israel idolatry in shituf is forbidden like outright idolatry, as it is stated (Shemot 22:19): "One who sacrifices to the gods, save to the Lord alone, shall be utterly destroyed." That is, a Jew who believes in God but also worshipped other gods besides God "shall be utterly destroyed," meaning he shall be put to death. For the Torah commanded Israel regarding faith in God's unity, as it is stated (Devarim 6:4): "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one." God likewise warned Israel in the Ten Commandments not to associate other idols in their faith, as it is stated (Shemot 20:2-5): "You shall have no other gods before Me. You shall not make for yourself a graven image… You shall not bow down to them nor serve them, for I the Lord your God am a jealous God…" Ramban explained (there) that this jealousy is directed specifically toward Israel, for Israel are His treasured people, whom He separated for Himself from all the peoples, as it is stated (Vayikra 20:26): "And I have separated you from the peoples to be Mine." And it is stated (Shemot 19:6): "And you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." Therefore, when Israel worship idols, God is jealous against them "as a man is jealous of his wife when she goes after others, and of his servant when he makes for himself another master."

This was the sin of Israel in the sin of the Golden Calf: they did not deny God and did not want to stop serving Him, but they associated idolatry as well. After they thought that Moshe Rabbeinu would not return from Mount Sinai, they reasoned that without him they could not be watched over directly by God, for He is too exalted, and in order to receive help they had to worship also one of the idols beneath Him. As it is stated (Shemot 32:1-4): "And the people saw that Moshe delayed to come down from the mountain, and the people gathered against Aharon and said to him: Rise, make us gods who shall go before us, for this Moshe, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him… And all the people took off the golden rings that were in their ears and brought them to Aharon. And he took it from their hand and fashioned it with a graving tool and made it a molten calf, and they said: These are your gods, O Israel…" And even though they continued to believe in God, since they associated idolatry, they became liable to death. Those who sinned before witnesses who had warned them were punished with death by the sword at the hands of the sons of Levi; those who sinned before witnesses who had not warned them died that same day in the plague with which God struck them; and all the rest were tested by drinking the water into which the calf had been ground, and the sinners died of a disease of the belly called dropsy (Yoma 66b; Rashi, Shemot 32:20).

However, the sin of Jews who worship idols in shituf is lighter than the sin of outright idol worshippers. As the Sages said, Israel did not become liable to annihilation for the sin of the Calf, because they continued to believe in God, as it is stated (Shemot 32:8): "And they said: These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up (he'elukha) out of the land of Egypt" – he'elukha is in the plural, meaning [they included] God as well (Sanhedrin 63a). We likewise learn that the sin of idol worshippers who do not associate the service of God is graver, as it is stated (Shoftim 10:6): "And the children of Israel again did evil in the eyes of the Lord, and served the Be'alim… and they forsook the Lord and did not serve Him." The Sages said (Eikha Rabba, Petiḥta 10): "'And did not serve Him' – not even in partnership," and therefore they were punished with extra severity.9

sections.title: The View of Those Lenient about Shituf for Bnei Noaḥ
sections.html:
The poskim disagree whether idolatry in shituf is forbidden to Bnei Noaḥ. That is, the prohibition of idolatry is one of the seven mitzvot of Bnei Noaḥ (above section 1), and the question is whether it also includes a prohibition against worshipping idols in shituf. On this question also depends the attitude toward believers in Christianity, who hold that "that man" too is God.

According to most poskim and commentators, although it is fitting for Bnei Noaḥ to believe in the faith of God's unity, only the people of Israel are obligated in this, as explained in the previous section. But Bnei Noaḥ are not forbidden to worship idols in shituf: as long as they believe that the Lord is the God of gods and also turn to Him in prayer, even if they associate belief in an additional idol, despite the error in this, they do not transgress the prohibition of idolatry. Similarly, we learned that the Torah warned Israel to destroy every idolatrous statue and not to benefit from it, whereas Bnei Noaḥ are not warned about this (section 4). For as long as they associate faith in God, there is no prohibition for them in keeping the statues, and consequently they need not destroy them. We also learned (section 3) that a sacrifice is not accepted from a Jew who worshipped idols, whereas from a ben Noaḥ who worshipped idols a sacrifice is accepted: since he comes to offer to God, he is associating faith in God, and he does not have the status of an idol worshipper. We also learned that Israel must give up their lives for faith in God's unity, whereas Bnei Noaḥ are not obligated in this (section 2). This is because as long as they also believe in God, they are not considered idol worshippers, and consequently need not give up their lives. Similarly, we learned that Israel are forbidden to make statues of angels, heavenly bodies and people for decoration, whereas for a ben Noaḥ there is no prohibition (section 5): since they are not forbidden to associate, as long as they also believe in God, they are not forbidden to make statues.

We also learn this from the fact that the Torah repeatedly warned Israel in a special way regarding faith in God's unity, as it is stated (Devarim 4:9-20): "Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life, and make them known to your children and your children's children. The day that you stood before the Lord your God at Ḥorev… Take good heed therefore of yourselves, for you saw no manner of form on the day that the Lord spoke to you at Ḥorev out of the midst of the fire, lest you deal corruptly and make yourselves a graven image… and lest you lift up your eyes to the heavens, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the host of heaven, you be drawn away and bow down to them and serve them, which the Lord your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven. But the Lord has taken you and brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be to Him a people of inheritance, as at this day." The Rishonim explained that since God did not reveal Himself to the nations of the world as He revealed Himself to Israel at the Sinai revelation, His governance of the world is reflected to them through the forces of nature, "which the Lord your God has allotted to all the peoples under the whole heaven." And since God bestows abundance upon each people and each land through stars, constellations and ministering powers, they are liable to attribute independent powers to them and to worship them (Rashbam, Ramban, Rashba and others). Most Aḥaronim learned from this that as long as they also believe in God as the supreme God, there is no prohibition in their associating belief in other idols as well.

The aspiration, however, is to purify faith of every trace of idolatry, and so it will be in the future, as it is stated (Zekharia 14:9): "And the Lord shall be King over all the earth; on that day the Lord shall be one and His Name one." But as long as the moral and spiritual situation is not suited to this, there is a concern that if Bnei Noaḥ do not believe at all, their moral situation may be worse. Therefore it is better that they believe in shituf, and thereby strengthen themselves against evil inclinations and murderousness, and progress gradually in the levels of faith and morality (see below chapter 9).10

sections.title: The View of Those Stringent about Shituf, and regarding Christians
sections.html:
On the other hand, some hold that just as idolatry in shituf is forbidden to Israel like outright idolatry, so it is forbidden to non-Jews. True, we learned that the Torah distanced Israel from idolatry and added commands for them in which Bnei Noaḥ are not commanded; however, in the essential prohibition of idolatry, Israel and Bnei Noaḥ are equal. For the Sages stated a rule (Sanhedrin 56b): "Regarding idolatry, the things for which a Jewish court executes – a ben Noaḥ is warned about them." And since a Jew who worshipped idols in shituf is liable to death, as it is stated (Shemot 22:19): "One who sacrifices to the gods, save to the Lord alone, shall be utterly destroyed," Bnei Noaḥ too are forbidden to worship idols in shituf, and one who worships in shituf is liable to death.

They further argued that if Bnei Noaḥ were permitted to worship idols in shituf, the prohibition of idolatry would be nullified for them, since all idol worshippers believe in some way in a primordial Creator who is above everything. As it is stated (Malakhi 1:11): "For from the rising of the sun to its setting My Name is great among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to My Name, and a pure offering, for My Name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts." The Sages explained that the meaning is that in all places, even the idol worshippers call God "the God of gods" (Menaḥot 110a), and nevertheless they are called idol worshippers (Me'il Tzedaka 22). Those who permit respond that if they hold that the primordial Creator does not influence the world, and they do not turn to Him in prayer, they are considered outright idol worshippers. But if they believe that the God of gods too influences the world and they also turn to Him in prayer, they are considered worshippers of idolatry in shituf.

Those who are stringent further derived that idolatry in shituf is forbidden to non-Jews from the fact that the Sages forbade doing business with Christians on Sunday and the three days before it, as with idol worshippers, even though Christians associate the Name of Heaven. True, the Rishonim permitted doing business with Christians in practice, but their main reason was that Christians are not devout, and because of [the risk of] enmity and the need for a livelihood, and not because they do not have the status of idol worshippers. Therefore the stringent poskim ruled that idolatry in shituf is forbidden to non-Jews, and Christians are considered idol worshippers.11

sections.title: The Lenient View and the Status of Christians and Hindus
sections.html: The view of most poskim, as halakha and in practice, is that non-Jews are not forbidden to worship idols in shituf. Therefore Christian non-Jews are not considered idol worshippers, since together with their belief in "that man" they believe in God. It seems that the same law applies to adherents of the Hindu religion, who in principle associate [with their gods] faith in a supreme God (see below 8:5, and at the end of the note here).12

sections.title: The Change in Attitude toward Christians, and the Status of the Minim
sections.html:
But we must explain why the Sages in the Talmud considered Christians idol worshippers, whereas in practice many of the Aḥaronim ruled that idolatry in shituf is permitted to Bnei Noaḥ, and therefore Christianity is not considered idolatry for them.

Three explanations can be offered, which combine with and complement one another. But before we explain them, let us preface that even one who does not accept these arguments will need to find another explanation for the fact that the Sages of the Talmud considered Christianity outright idolatry, whereas most poskim ruled that Christianity is idolatry in shituf and permitted to Bnei Noaḥ, and some even hold that it is not idolatry at all, as cited in the next section.

The first explanation: at first many Christians were Jews or converts, and according to all opinions shituf is forbidden to Jews like outright idolatry; therefore there was no room to be lenient in their case on the basis that they associate the Name of Heaven.

The second: since Christianity turned to idol worshippers, those who became Christians revered mainly "that man" and the statues they saw in churches. And although the Tanakh was the foundational book of their religion, and their scholars also turned to God who revealed Himself to the prophets of Israel, since almost all Christians, including some of the monks, could not read, their reverence was mainly for the statues of "that man," like all idol worshippers who revered statues, and therefore they were considered idol worshippers. Over time, in a gradual process, more and more Christians rose to associate the Name of Heaven, that is, to emphasise also faith in God as explained in the Tanakh. In parallel, we find many of the great Rishonim who raised the argument to be lenient regarding Christians, that they are worshippers of idolatry in shituf. But since the faith of the Christian masses still remained essentially idolatrous, and their reverence was for the statues of "that man," they did not decide to regard them as worshippers of idolatry in shituf. Later, many learned to read, and their reading of the Tanakh intensified their faith in God, and more Christians began to direct their worship to God, who forbade idolatry and the making of statues. As part of this process, in the year 5277 (1517), the Protestant stream crystallised within Christianity; it removed all the statues from the churches and broke them, leaving only the crosses as an image to which they bow. In parallel, in the Catholic stream too, which left the statues in place, faith in God as explained in the Tanakh intensified, and Christian scholars explained that the statues are symbols. Following this, in the period of the Aḥaronim it was ruled that Christianity is idolatry in shituf, and since most rabbis ruled that Bnei Noaḥ are not forbidden to worship idols in shituf, they regarded Christians as not being idol worshippers.

The third: since Christianity emerged from within Judaism and challenged the foundations of the faith and Torah of Israel, it posed an especially grave threat to Judaism, and therefore the Sages defined it as minut (heresy), from which one must keep away as from outright idolatry. Therefore, even when it was clear that the people in question were non-Jews who associated the Name of Heaven in their worship, they were stringent and regarded them as idol worshippers. But after many generations, when Christianity had moved away from Judaism and it was already clear that it was a different religion, and the vast majority of its believers were entirely non-Jewish, they returned to the basic law that Bnei Noaḥ are not forbidden to worship idols in shituf, and consequently they did not regard Christians who associated the Name of Heaven as idol worshippers. And as long as they did not try to convert Jews to Christianity, they did not regard them as minim.13

sections.title: Those Who Hold That Christianity Is Not Idolatry
sections.html:
Some say that Christianity is not idolatry at all, not even in shituf, for Christian scholars repeatedly and emphatically claim that they believe in the faith of God's unity as explained in the Torah. According to them, the Trinity in which they believe is nothing but three manifestations of the one God, and one of the three manifestations is through "that man." And since, according to them, belief in the Trinity and in "that man" does not nullify faith in God's unity, then even though this involves a great distortion and an internal contradiction, such a belief is nevertheless not considered idolatry. Similarly regarding the statues and crosses: since according to Christian scholars divinity is not embodied in them, but they are only symbols, they are not considered idolatrous statues and images.

However, according to most poskim the law does not depend on a precise clarification of the view of Christian scholars, but on what the Christian masses believe and do. And since in practice the Christian masses, including priests, believe that "that man" is actually God, and bow down to images out of belief that divinity is embodied in them, they therefore regarded Christianity as idolatry in shituf.14

sections.title: Those Who Hold That Decent Christians Have the Status of Ger Toshav
sections.html:
Rav Menaḥem Ha-Meiri explained two principles regarding Christians: first, that Christianity is not considered idolatry in shituf but a faith in God containing severe distortions, as we learned in the previous section. Second, that peoples who conduct themselves according to the ways of morality and decency, and have established laws for that purpose, are considered gerei toshav who keep the seven mitzvot of Bnei Noaḥ, and there is a mitzva to honour them and help them as much as possible.

With the first principle the vast majority of poskim did not agree. But with the second principle many of the great Aḥaronim of Israel agreed, and in their view, since Bnei Noaḥ are not forbidden to worship idols in shituf, Christianity is not forbidden to them; consequently, if they conduct themselves according to the customs of morality and decency, their status is that of gerei toshav, whom there is a mitzva to honour and help. So wrote our master Rav Kook: "that the main view is like the opinion of Meiri, that all the peoples who are bounded by decent conventions between man and his fellow are already considered gerei toshav in all human obligations" (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 89).15
